explanations.explanation: Silent it is, baker. The LORD says, “Be silent before Me, O islands…” (Isaiah 41:1). Think of a room going quiet right before somebody important starts to talk. Nobody plans that hush. It just happens.

Glad is a nice thought, but that's not the word here. The LORD says, “Be silent before Me, O islands…” (Isaiah 41:1). This is a summons, and I've never heard of anybody getting a summons and a party hat in the same envelope. The islands are called to quiet down and come forward.

Ready sounds right, friend, and you're in the neighborhood. The LORD does say, “…let the peoples renew their strength.” (Isaiah 41:1). But the word before that is “silent.” First comes the quiet, and then they come forward.

True, baker. The one from the east is not stuck standing around. The LORD says, “He hands nations over to him and subdues kings before him.” (Isaiah 41:2). He's moving, and the kings are the ones getting handled.

This one is actually true, friend. The LORD says the one from the east gets nations handed over to him, and that He “…subdues kings before him.” (Isaiah 41:2). So the kings in his way are the ones being subdued. I know a sentence like that can make you second-guess everything.

Close, but it's the other direction, baker. The text says, “He pursues them, going on safely, hardly touching the path with his feet.” (Isaiah 41:3). He's the one chasing, and he's not dragging anything. Nobody who's struggling to keep up has feet that barely touch the ground.

False is right, friend. The text says, “He pursues them, going on safely, hardly touching the path with his feet.” (Isaiah 41:3). He's the one doing the chasing, and nothing there says he's dragging or struggling. Feet that hardly touch the path and a man going on safely sound like someone moving with ease.

The LORD Himself, baker. He asks who performed all this and carried it out, then answers it in His own voice with “…I am He.” (Isaiah 41:4). Calling forth the generations from the beginning is His work. Nobody else steps up to the microphone.

I see why you'd pick him, friend. He's the busy one in the picture. But the LORD is the One asking who stirred him up in the first place (Isaiah 41:2). The answer comes back, “…I am He.” (Isaiah 41:4), so the credit goes to the LORD.

Not the kings of the islands, baker. The question is who performed this and carried it out, calling forth the generations from the beginning. The LORD answers it Himself with “…I am He.” (Isaiah 41:4). Nobody else gets named as the answer.
Fear, baker. The text says, “The islands see and fear; the ends of the earth tremble.” (Isaiah 41:5). The islands see, and fear is what comes next. They also approach and come forward.

Rejoice is a happy guess, friend, but the text says something else. “The islands see and fear; the ends of the earth tremble.” (Isaiah 41:5). Rejoicing comes up later in this passage, and it belongs to Israel (Isaiah 41:16). The islands are the ones trembling.

Scattering makes sense if you're scared, baker. But the text says, “They approach and come forward.” (Isaiah 41:5). They fear and the ends of the earth tremble, and still they approach. I'd have scattered at the first sign of trouble.

Be strong, baker. “Each one helps the other and says to his brother, ‘Be strong!’” (Isaiah 41:6). It's people lifting each other up while the ends of the earth tremble. Everybody needs a friend like that in the moment.
You'd expect that after all the trembling, friend. But look at what the text says. Each one says to his brother, “Be strong!” (Isaiah 41:6). They're helping each other, not running from each other.
That's a gloomy one, baker, and the text doesn't go there. Each one helps the other and says to his brother, “Be strong!” (Isaiah 41:6). It's encouragement in the air, not surrender.

Nail it down, baker. “He nails it down so it will not be toppled.” (Isaiah 41:7). Just before that, the one who wields the hammer cheers on the one who strikes the anvil, saying of the welding, “It is good.” When I really want my cookie boxes to stay shut, I'm not shy with the tape either.

Praying is a good habit, friend, but this verse doesn't mention it. What it says is, “He nails it down so it will not be toppled.” (Isaiah 41:7). It's a workshop scene, with hammers and an anvil. The crew is making sure the thing stays standing.
A hill is a fine spot, baker, but the text never puts it there. The verse says, “He nails it down so it will not be toppled.” (Isaiah 41:7). A nail is what keeps it from toppling.
My friend, baker. The LORD says, “…descendant of Abraham My friend—” (Isaiah 41:8). Abraham was Israel's ancestor, and that's the name the LORD gives him here. I'd take that title over any trophy.

Firstborn sounds official, friend, but it isn't what the LORD says here. He says, “…descendant of Abraham My friend—” (Isaiah 41:8). Firstborn would be about rank, and “friend” is about closeness. I think that's a better title than any rank.

Shepherd has a nice ring to it, baker, but it's not the word for Abraham here. The LORD says, “…descendant of Abraham My friend—” (Isaiah 41:8). The title is “friend,” plain and warm. I'd happily take that one from the LORD myself.
The second half trips this one up, friend. The LORD says, “I have chosen and not rejected you.” (Isaiah 41:9). So He chose them, and He didn't reject them. The statement has it backward.

False, baker. The LORD says, “You are My servant.” Then He adds, “I have chosen and not rejected you.” (Isaiah 41:9). His choosing and His not rejecting go together. That's good news you can build a day on.
He is with them, baker. “Do not fear, for I am with you; do not be afraid, for I am your God.” (Isaiah 41:10). The reason isn't a plan or a number. It's the LORD being right there with them.
That's the kind of reason people usually reach for, friend. But the LORD never mentions an army here. He says, “Do not fear, for I am with you…” (Isaiah 41:10). His own presence is the reason.

Walls would feel safe, baker, but they don't show up in this verse. The LORD says, “Do not fear, for I am with you; do not be afraid, for I am your God.” (Isaiah 41:10). He points to Himself as the reason, not to any stonework.

Strengthen is the word, baker, and the verse says it first. The LORD says, “I will strengthen you; I will surely help you; I will uphold you with My righteous right hand.” (Isaiah 41:10). Strength, help and upholding all come in one breath. Hard to ask for a better promise.
Test is a tough word, friend, and it isn't the one here. The LORD says, “I will strengthen you; I will surely help you…” (Isaiah 41:10). It's a promise about help, not about a quiz.

Hide sounds like tucking someone away, baker, but that's not what He says. The LORD says, “I will strengthen you; I will surely help you…” (Isaiah 41:10). He's promising strength and help, right out in the open.

explanations.answer: They will be ashamed and disgraced
explanations.explanation: Ashamed and disgraced, baker. “Behold, all who rage against you will be ashamed and disgraced; those who contend with you will be reduced to nothing and will perish.” (Isaiah 41:11). The ones raging against Israel don't come out on top. It's the LORD's promise to His people.

That's the opposite of what the LORD says, friend. He says those who rage against Israel “…will be ashamed and disgraced…” (Isaiah 41:11). Nobody in that group ends up ruling. They're reduced to nothing.

It would make a sweet ending, baker, but the verse doesn't say that. The LORD says, “those who contend with you will be reduced to nothing and will perish.” (Isaiah 41:11). So the raging ones are ashamed and disgraced.

True, baker. The LORD says, “You will seek them but will not find them.” (Isaiah 41:12). Israel looks for those who waged war against them, and there's nothing left to find. Those enemies come to nothing.

This one is actually true, friend. The LORD says, “You will seek them but will not find them. Those who wage war against you will come to nothing.” (Isaiah 41:12). So Israel does go looking, and the search comes up empty.

The Holy One of Israel, baker. The LORD says, “Your Redeemer is the Holy One of Israel.” (Isaiah 41:14). Right before that He says, “Do not fear, O Jacob, you worm, O few men of Israel.” Then He names who stands behind them, and that name is worth remembering.

He's been in the spotlight, friend, but he isn't the Redeemer. The LORD says, “Your Redeemer is the Holy One of Israel.” (Isaiah 41:14). The one from the east was stirred up by the LORD (Isaiah 41:2).

Abraham does get a kind title earlier, baker, when the LORD calls him “My friend” (Isaiah 41:8). But the Redeemer is somebody else. The LORD says, “Your Redeemer is the Holy One of Israel.” (Isaiah 41:14).

Old and dull is the opposite, baker. The LORD says, “…I will make you into a threshing sledge, new and sharp, with many teeth.” (Isaiah 41:15). Brand new, sharp, and lots of teeth. That's a tool made to get things done.
False, friend. The LORD says, “…I will make you into a threshing sledge, new and sharp, with many teeth.” (Isaiah 41:15). Nothing worn out about it. A sledge like that can thresh mountains.

Rejoice in the LORD, baker. “But you will rejoice in the LORD; you will glory in the Holy One of Israel.” (Isaiah 41:16). The wind carries the chaff off, and Israel's joy goes to the LORD. The glory goes to Him too.

That's an easy thing to do after a win, friend, but it's not what the text says. “But you will rejoice in the LORD; you will glory in the Holy One of Israel.” (Isaiah 41:16). That comes right after the wind carries the chaff away. Their glory is in Him, not in themselves.

Mourning over the mountains isn't in the text, baker. “But you will rejoice in the LORD; you will glory in the Holy One of Israel.” (Isaiah 41:16). That comes right after the wind carries the chaff away and a gale scatters it. The response the text gives is rejoicing.

True, baker. The LORD says, “I, the LORD, will answer them; I, the God of Israel, will not forsake them.” (Isaiah 41:17). The poor and needy are parched, and He promises not to forsake them. That's a promise worth holding onto.

This one is true, friend. The LORD says of the poor and needy, “I, the LORD, will answer them; I, the God of Israel, will not forsake them.” (Isaiah 41:17). Their tongues are parched with thirst, and He says He will answer them. So True is the one that matches the text.

Desert is the one, baker. The LORD says, “I will turn the desert into a pool of water, and the dry land into flowing springs.” (Isaiah 41:18). A desert becomes a pool of water. The dry land gets flowing springs too, and that's quite a change.
A sea is already full of water, friend, so there's nothing to turn. The LORD says, “I will turn the desert into a pool of water…” (Isaiah 41:18). The dry place is the one that gets the water.

City isn't in that verse, baker. The LORD says, “I will turn the desert into a pool of water…” (Isaiah 41:18). Nothing in that line turns a city into anything. The dry land gets flowing springs, and that's the change the verse promises.

explanations.answer: So all will know the LORD did it
explanations.explanation: That's it, baker. The LORD says it's “…so that all may see and know, may consider and understand, that the hand of the LORD has done this and the Holy One of Israel has created it.” (Isaiah 41:20). Every river and every tree points back to Him. He wants everyone to see whose hand did it.

explanations.answer: So Israel can build new cities
explanations.explanation: That's a practical idea, friend, but the text doesn't give it as the reason. The LORD says it's “…so that all may see and know, may consider and understand, that the hand of the LORD has done this…” (Isaiah 41:20). The point is that all would know it was His hand.

explanations.answer: So the nations will fear Israel
explanations.explanation: Fearing Israel isn't the reason given, baker. The LORD says it's “…so that all may see and know, may consider and understand, that the hand of the LORD has done this and the Holy One of Israel has created it.” (Isaiah 41:20). Attention goes to the LORD's hand, not to Israel.
